content: Benzphetamine is a sympathomimetic amine that has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of exogenous obesity. It is intended for short-term use as an adjunct to a calorie-restricted weight reduction regimen. The potential benefits of this medication must be carefully weighed against the risks associated with its use. Common adverse reactions to benzphetamine include increased blood pressure, palpitations, tachyarrhythmia, urticaria, diarrhea, nausea, an unpleasant taste in the mouth, dry mouth (xerostomia), central nervous system stimulation, overstimulation, dizziness, headache, insomnia, tremor, depression following drug withdrawal, restlessness, and changes in libido. Adult Indications and Dosage Benzphetamine hydrochloride tablets are indicated for the management of exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct (a few weeks) in a weight reduction program based on caloric restriction. The limited usefulness of this class of drugs should be weighed against the potential risks inherent in their use. Pediatric Indications and Dosage There is limited information regarding the FDA-labeled use of benzphetamine in pediatric patients. Its use is not recommended in individuals under 12 years of age. Contraindications Benzphetamine hydrochloride tablets are contraindicated in patients with advanced arteriosclerosis, symptomatic cardiovascular disease, moderate to severe hypertension, hyperthyroidism, known hypersensitivity or idiosyncrasy to sympathomimetic amines, and glaucoma. It should not be administered to patients in an agitated state or those with a history of drug abuse. Hypertensive crises have been reported when sympathomimetic amines are used concomitantly or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Benzphetamine should not be used with other central nervous system stimulants. Pregnancy and Nursing Benzphetamine hydrochloride tablets may cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman. Amphetamines have been shown to be teratogenic and embryotoxic in mammals at high multiples of the human dose. This medication is contraindicated in women who are pregnant or may become pregnant. If used during pregnancy or if the patient becomes pregnant while taking this drug, the patient should be informed of the potential hazard to the fetus. Amphetamines are excreted in human milk, and nursing mothers should be advised to refrain from breastfeeding while taking this medication. Warnings and Precautions When tolerance to the anorectic effect develops, the recommended dose should not be exceeded in an attempt to increase the effect; instead, the drug should be discontinued. Insulin requirements in diabetes mellitus may be altered with the use of anorexigenic drugs and concomitant dietary restrictions. Psychological disturbances have been reported in patients receiving anorectic agents in combination with a restrictive dietary regimen. Caution should be exercised when prescribing amphetamines to patients with mild hypertension. The smallest feasible amount should be prescribed or dispensed at one time to minimize the possibility of overdose. Adverse Reactions Adverse reactions associated with benzphetamine include palpitations, tachycardia, and elevated blood pressure. Isolated reports of cardiomyopathy have been associated with chronic amphetamine use. Other reactions include overstimulation, restlessness, dizziness, insomnia, tremor, sweating, headache, and, rarely, psychotic episodes at recommended doses. Depression may occur following drug withdrawal. Gastrointestinal disturbances such as dry mouth, unpleasant taste, nausea, diarrhea, and urticaria have also been reported. Changes in libido may occur. Overdosage Acute overdose with amphetamines may result in restlessness, tremor, rapid breathing (tachypnea), confusion, aggressiveness, panic states, fatigue, and depression. Cardiovascular effects include arrhythmias, hypertension or hypotension, and circulatory collapse. Gastrointestinal symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. Hyperpyrexia and rhabdomyolysis have been reported and can lead to complications. Fatal poisoning is usually preceded by convulsions and coma. Management of acute amphetamine intoxication is largely symptomatic and may include sedation with a barbiturate. Acidification of the urine increases amphetamine excretion. Pharmacology Benzphetamine hydrochloride is a sympathomimetic amine with pharmacologic activity similar to amphetamines. Its actions include central nervous system stimulation and elevation of blood pressure. Tachyphylaxis and tolerance have been demonstrated with all drugs of this class. These drugs, commonly referred to as anorectics or anorexigenics, are used in obesity management. However, it has not been established that their primary action in treating obesity is appetite suppression; other central nervous system actions or metabolic effects may be involved. Use in Specific Populations Geriatric Use: There is no FDA guidance on the use of benzphetamine in geriatric patients. Gender and Race: There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of benzphetamine in relation to gender or racial populations. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: There is no FDA guidance on the use of benzphetamine in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Immunocompromised Patients: There is no FDA guidance on the use of benzphetamine in immunocompromised patients. Administration and Monitoring Benzphetamine is administered orally. There is limited information regarding monitoring requirements for this medication. Storage Store at 25°C (77°F), with excursions permitted to 15°-30°C (59°-86°F). Dispense in a tight, light-resistant container as defined in the USP. Abuse and Dependence Benzphetamine is a controlled substance under Schedule III of the Controlled Substances Act. Amphetamines and related stimulant drugs have been extensively abused, and the potential for abuse of benzphetamine should be considered when evaluating its use in a weight reduction program. Abuse may lead to intense psychological dependence and severe social dysfunction. Abrupt cessation following prolonged high-dose administration may result in extreme fatigue and mental depression. Patient Counseling Patients should be cautioned that amphetamines may impair their ability to engage in potentially hazardous activities such as operating machinery or driving. Alcohol interaction with benzphetamine has not been established, and patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while taking this medication.
